title: Dark mode as a system decision
metaTitle: Dark mode design system, decided in pairs
excerpt: Dark mode is a second set of color decisions, planned with the light palette. A filter at the end inverts the product instead of designing the pairs.
alt: A long, quiet office corridor with glass rooms, a teal sofa, and a dark kitchen. The dark kitchen was designed as a room, which is what a second palette should feel like.

faqs.question: Should dark mode be an invert filter?
faqs.answer: Plan it as a second set of color pairs, written down with the light palette. An invert filter also flips photographs, hairlines, and focus rings. Check each pair for readable text and a visible focus ring before the theme ships.

faqs.question: When should a small team skip dark mode?
faqs.answer: Skip it when the product is a single light page and nobody is asking to use it in the dark. A second palette is real work, and a thin invert creates a theme you will have to remove. Build the pairs when people stay in the product for long sessions, or when another product is about to copy the first.

faqs.question: Where should the two palettes live?
faqs.answer: Give each color job one name and two values, light and dark. Keep those names in the design file and in the code the components already read. A raw hex value inside a component will miss the switch and leave a light-colored island on a dark page.

markdown:
A dark mode design system is a second set of color decisions, planned with the light palette. Each job the color does in daylight needs a partner for a dark surface: background, text, line, accent, and the focus ring. A filter applied at the end inverts values the product never chose, and the interface looks stained.

Write both rows before the first screen ships. The person who switches themes should recognize the product. They should not have to relearn which color means action and which color means danger.

## Decide the pairs before the screens

Start when you choose the brand colors. Make a table with two columns, light and dark, and one row per job. Page background. Raised surface, such as a card. Primary text. Muted text. Hairline. Accent. The label that sits on the accent. A destructive color, if the product can fail in a way people must notice.

Pick the dark background as a color, the way you picked the light one. A near-black with a trace of the brand usually feels like the same room with the lights lowered. Pure black, or a brand color simply flipped, usually feels like a different product. The picture to keep in mind is a corridor that was designed with a dark kitchen at the end of it. The dark room is a room. It is not daylight with the lamps forced off.

If dark mode is not shipping in this release, leave the second column in the file with a note. An empty column is a reminder that the decision is still open. A missing column is how the theme arrives later as a weekend experiment.

## What an invert filter breaks

A filter takes each hex value and flips it. Dark text becomes light, which is sometimes acceptable. A photograph flips too, which ruins the picture. A soft gray hairline becomes a bright stripe. A pale warning tint becomes a heavy color that no longer means warning. Shadows, which on a light page are slightly darker than the surface, turn into glows. Elevation is a relationship between layers. A filter only knows arithmetic.

Focus suffers in the same pass. A ring that was a clear stroke on a light button can disappear on the inverted button, or it can shout over the label. Status colors drift off their meaning. The green that meant success in the light theme becomes whatever green the math produced.

The W3C's [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) organize WCAG 2.2 under four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. A theme switch is a perceivable and operable change. Text has to stay readable on the new surface, and the control that shows keyboard focus has to stay visible. Check those conditions on each pair. Do not expect an invert step to satisfy them.

## The pairs that carry the product

You can postpone a dark version of every marketing illustration. You cannot postpone the interface people use for a session.

- Page and surface. The card should separate from the page. On a dark theme that usually means a slightly lighter surface, not a heavier shadow.
- Primary text and muted text. Muted text is where dark themes fail quietly. A gray that was soft on white can vanish on a dark background.
- Hairline and focus. The line that separates fields and the ring that shows focus have to be visible, and distinct from each other.
- Accent and the label on it. A filled button needs a label color chosen for that fill in both themes. A white label may work on both. A dark label often will not.
- Status. Success, warning, and danger keep their roles. Test them on both backgrounds before they spread into badges and toasts.

Photographs stay as they were shot. Charts get their own series colors, tested on both backgrounds. Neither should run through the invert used on the chrome.

## Where the pairs live

Give each job one name and two values. In Figma, a variable collection with two modes is enough for a small team. In the repository, the same names resolve to the light or dark value when the theme changes. The button does not know that it is dark. It uses the accent token, and the token changes.

Hanabi builds interfaces in React, TypeScript, and Tailwind, so the practical form is a small theme the components already read. Adding a dark mode should mean filling the second value, not restyling each screen. If a component has a raw hex value inside it, that value will miss the switch and leave a light-colored island on a dark page.

Follow the system preference when the person has asked their device for a dark appearance. Add a manual toggle only when switching is part of the work, such as a tool people keep open for long sessions. A marketing site can follow the preference and skip the toggle until someone asks for it.

The rule for anything new fits in one sentence: a color is not done until it has a partner. Review the partner on the same screen, side by side. If you cannot see the focus ring, the muted label, and the accent button in both modes, the pair is not ready to ship.

## When to wait, and when the second column is due

Wait if the product is a single light page and nobody is asking to use it in the dark. A second palette is real work. Shipping a thin invert to look current creates a theme you will have to apologize for, or quietly remove.

Build the pairs when people use the product for long sessions, when the identity already includes a dark surface, or when a second product is about to copy the first. The cost of the second column now is a few extra rows in the token table. The cost later is a search for every hard-coded value, plus a week of screenshots that do not match.

Keep the two columns on the same names. If light and dark drift onto different words, you have two systems. The piece that covers those names is [tokens, type, and the decisions that stop visual drift](/blog/tokens-type-and-drift). Read it next if the palette is still a list of hex values pasted into frames.

When you want both palettes designed and built with the product, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The studio treats a dark theme as a set of decisions recorded with the rest of the system.
